### Show the distributions of values visually. Explain, in comments, what those distributions mean statistically. Be thorough.
```{r}
# path is hard coded to dataset, can easily replace with your path
data <- read.csv(
  "C:\\Users\\Gabe\\Documents\\GitHub\\data_science_classes_windows\\data\\sales_data_sample.csv"
)


# display the first 6 rows of the data
head(data)

# print each column with its type - str is structure of data
str(data)


# aes() - Aesthetic mapping. It defines how data variables are represented visually in the plot.
# For example, mapping X to dates and Y to sales values.

# Another use of aes() is mapping y to ..density.., which shows the density of the data
# rather than the raw counts in the histogram.

# Density is calculated as a normalized value, not simply the proportion of a bin's count.
# The formula for density is:

# Density = Count of items in bin / (Bin width * Total number of items)

# Sets TotalSales as the variable on the X-axis.

# geom_histogram() uses aes() to map data variables to the visual components of the histogram.

#! Remember, ggplot takes the first arg as data, then we reference individual columns, similar to data$Column


# Get the number of rows
number_of_rows <- nrow(data)
sqrt_number_of_rows <- round(sqrt(number_of_rows))
sqrt_number_of_rows


#! We use plus operator to add layers
ggplot(data, aes(x = TotalSales)) +
  #! Histogram takes 2 portions: the density (usually on the y), and then bins. Bins are subjective, but a good rule is to make them relative to the number of data points. More specifically, square root of the data. 
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = ..density..),
    bins = sqrt_number_of_rows,
    fill = "skyblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3, fill = "red") + # add density layer for a smooth curve.  alpha is just opacity, but I noticed that when we change bin number, we can get the curve to appear above the bars
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Sales", x = "Total Sales", y = "Density")
# Again, the y-axis should display # Density = Count of items in bin / (Bin width * Total number of items)

# We can invert the graphs

```

Show the values of central tendency, both numerically and visually. Interpret those values in your own words in Markdown.

```{r}


# Measures of Central Tendency:
# - Mean: The average of all values.
# - Median: The middle value when the data is sorted.
# - Mode: The most frequently occurring value.




library(tidyverse)

# Calculate key metrics
central_tendency <- data %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(TotalSales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(TotalSales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mode = {
      freq_table <- table(TotalSales)
      as.numeric(names(freq_table)[which.max(freq_table)])
    }
  )

# Print results
central_tendency

```

Visually depict the Interquartile range. Interpret the IQR for the dataset (in Markdown).

```{r}

# Convert OrderDate to Date format (optional, for other analyses)
data$OrderDate <- as.Date(data$OrderDate, format = "%m/%d/%Y")

# Boxplot for TotalSales
boxplot(
  data$TotalSales,
  main = "Boxplot of Total Sales",
  ylab = "Total Sales",
  col = "lightblue",
  border = "darkblue"
)

# Calculate IQR
iqr_value <- IQR(data$TotalSales)
iqr_value


```

Create the statistics moments for the dataset.

```{r}


# Statistical moments are numerical values that describe the shape and characteristics of a distribution.
# While the concept may be less familiar outside of statistics, they're quite intuitive:
#
# - Mean: The average of the values (1st moment)
# - Variance: The spread of the data around the mean (2nd moment)
# - Skewness: The asymmetry of the distribution (3rd moment)
# - Kurtosis: The "fatness" of the tails — tells us whether the distribution has heavier or lighter tails
#             compared to a normal (Gaussian) distribution. This is often easier to interpret visually using line charts.


```

# Binning is the process of grouping continuous data into discrete intervals, or "bins."
# For example, if values range from 0 to 100, counting each individual value may not be useful.
# Instead, binning groups similar values into categories to better understand the distribution.
#
# We can experiment with different numbers of bins—such as 5, 10, 20, or 30—to see how it affects the shape
